editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: I was living in Parma, Ohio, with my mom and dad and younger sister and older brother at 7120 Thornton (ph) Drive, to be exact. And I went to high school at Parma High. And I went on to night school for a while. Worked at Warner Swayze doing war work and then of course I entered in the service in '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, indeed I do. My boyfriend and I were -- By the way, what you say, this is picked up too, your questions are picked up?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes, yes, it is loud enough.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Sensitive enough. He and I were ready to go down and see a movie, and I was listening to the radio when he came over. And my dad was going to let me use his car which was unusual. And we just sat in the living room for an hour or two, wondering where in the hell Pearl Harbor was. We just didn't know, of course, you know. Oh, yes, I remember that very distinctly. Castles come crashing down with the draft and whatnot.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you out of school at that point?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes. I graduated from school in 1940. Because I am 81 now -- will be in another month. Yes. And I wanted to go on to school, but then I just went to night school after that, and I figured why get heavily involved.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You said you were doing war work?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes. Warner Swayze at the time made Warner and Swayze turret lathes. And I went through an accelerated apprenticeship program called the Learner (ph) Program, so I know a little bit of background of the factory worker and the continual battle between unions and management. That was the only time I was a union man. But to be perfectly frank, after that I was in management. And I'll tell you right now that all the problems started were caused by the unions. Trust me on that. Trust me on that. I attained different positions in civil life in the unions on up to superintendent. And management has to accept their fair share indeed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say you were drafted then?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: I took the exam for the air corps and while I was waiting for the results I was drafted. And nothing happened for a couple of months. And I was a plodding private at Jefferson Barracks, Missouri, which is a Civil War post. I don't know whether you are aware of that or not. And I was loading -- in fact I'll tell you what I told a man just the other day. I was helping unload frozen chicken from boxcars that came in from the Philadelphia quartermaster depot, and it said "Frozen Chicken 1927." And this was 1942. Think about that. So we were saving -- we were preparing -- I guess every democratic nation does, stores a supply of food. They have to, but I never really thought about it until I saw it myself. I was getting kind of upset because I thought I was a little bit better, I didn't have to be a dough boy, a dough foot. I could lead, direct, and things like that. So I did what I thought was a dumb thing. I went to the library at Jefferson Barracks, Missouri, a magnificent brick building in Civil War days, as you can imagine. It was a Sunday morning after church, and there was a sergeant librarian, and I asked him if I could get a book on how to write a military letter. And he spent about 30 seconds ridiculing me why I wanted to do that. And I said well, I would like to, if I may, so he gave me a book. It was the officer's guide. I was just a (buck) private. He said you can't take this out. I said well, I understand that. So I wrote down how to write a military letter. And I came back to the barracks among other screaming men. And then I wrote a letter to commanding general of the Second Corps Army. At that time I didn't even know who the hell he was but to look into what happened to my records, and I did want to fly. I am capable. I can do it. And I mailed it. And in a week or two went by, and I heard nothing, and I was very disgusted, and I thought this was the end. So then in the interim I was transferred to Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts. There was a new army camp there and an air base where the fighter pilots were training. And I was transferred there. And I thought, well, letters will never catch up. I'm finished, you know. I am dog meat. And we were drilling out on the parade ground, the coldest place on earth, Chicopee Falls, Massachusetts, in January '43. Oh, God, it was cold. And a Jeep come wandering across the field. And driving the Jeep was a corporal, who wasn't very polite or bright. He walked up to the sergeant drilling us and said something to him, and the sergeant said private Private Belovich, front and center. I thought oh, golly, something happened to Mom and Dad, you know, maybe my dog too. And I said yes. He says were you in town all weekend. I said no, I was not. He said I didn't think so. You are not the type. But the corporal here says the company commander wants to see you. I thought geez, my folks. Got in this Jeep, and the corporal started to verbally abuse me. He said all you draftees are all alike. And I just let him rant.And we got in. It was a good mile drive, too, to the company commander's. And my barracks happened to be right next to the day room where his office was. He was a nice guy. He was a basketball coach at John Carroll, Joe Hocktor (ph), a wonderful guy. And he leaned over the desk, smiled, and he says you son of a bitch. I swear. He says why didn't you tell me you had an uncle who was two star. And then it hit me. The letter went through. But I said -- I started to say that I don't have -- I understand. I understand, Tom. You did all right. Anyway, I have got a twist here. Got to get your butt under training and send you to the classification center in Tennessee, Nashville -- or was it Memphis? Nashville, yeah, Nashville, Tennessee. And I thought my (dicks) came through. So to make a long story short, I went through training, fell right into it. I was commissioned a bombardier a little over a year later, a year and a half later. I was a second lieutenant, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything you can tell me about your training, any interesting stories about that?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: There are a lot of nice people there. Good people. Good straightforward people. And the interesting thing about it, yes, in my class there were only two people who were college graduates as opposed to what it is today. And one of them was Joe Vodka (ph), who was from Cleveland. I didn't know him at the time. He was 24 years old. I was 21, 22. And we were Catholic and met at church and whatnot. We got to talking. And we both made it. And we double dated when we were sent home. Each had a ten-day leave. And he was an only child. And he is now buried over at St. Marys Cemetery on Clark Avenue. He went down in one of the Castle raids. He was there about four minutes ahead of us over the target. We used to check on each other on the radio or ground when we got in. And I knew it was him. But it was one of those terrible things where you know it, but his mom and dad don't know it, neither does his fiancee. So you sit on that waiting for formal rules and regulations to apply. But he went down, I think it was about -- He was in a different bomber group than I was, of course. He was just up the road. Bomber groups were close together, located close together. And I often wonder -- I never saw his fiancee after that. A year later I returned from overseas and visited his folks and whatnot. I didn't know too many details and, of course, if I did I wouldn't have told them. But that was probably -- Today they refer to that as traumatic experience. In those days it just scared the living feces out of you, you know. But he was a nice guy, tall blonde. I still have his picture some place. He was about six one or six two, and his fiancee was a tall lovely young lady too. And I was dating at that time a dark-haired English -- Irish girl, lovely little thing. But she sent me a dear John letter, and we went our separate ways.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got that when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yes, well, I was about two weeks prior to going overseas I got the dear John letter. Geez, I couldn't believe what I was reading. But I had no intention of getting serious. Hell, I was only 21 years old, and she was 19, you know. But, fortunately, I met Helen a few years later, and it worked out fine. We had five kids.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So specifically what kinds of things did you do in bombardier training?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Well, learn the ins and outs of the bomb and navigation and learn how to run that complicated Norton bomb sight, because at that time the Norton bomb sight was being connected and engineered to the automatic pilot so that the bombardier actually flew the airplane by turning certain knobs on the instrument. And we learned how to do that and operate that equipment and trim up the aircraft [Clock chimes]

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Back to the bombardier training.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Where did I leave off?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think that you were talking about the Norton bomb sight?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, the Norton bomb sight, yes. It was a fantastic instrument, but you had to have a good pilot and good aircraft and ideal weather conditions, and most of the time we didn't have that. We had to do the best we could. But from the pictures I have seen of the destruction of Europe, we did a fine job. We destroyed their ability to wage war, which is what we were supposed to do.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were assigned the B-24 so at the beginning there when you started flying?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah. We called them, I think I mentioned over the phone, B-crash 24. We called it banana boat, slap-sided aerial truck and whatnot. But we loved the aircraft, because it was anywhere from to 40 to 60 miles an hour faster than the B-17, and it carried an extra ton. And that was the bombardier's ambition; the more tonnage you get on the target, the hell, the better things will be. You can get out of this mess, you know. And it did not fly slow for landing as you would like. It had that famous Davis airfoil on it, and you had to get that sucker up to 135 miles an hour on the ground before she would even think about flying. And then as the aircraft began to gain speed, just like some of the new jets we have, the wings began to bend as they are picking up the weight. Some of them would bend a foot, foot and a half, you know, and then flap. We talked to the tech reps on the ground, civilian engineers who were there, and they said well, they are supposed to flap like that. And I said golly, that much? You know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were there many accidents during training on those?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes. There was one I remember distinctly. I was at the base theater that evening at Colorado Springs, which by now is the home of the Air Force Academy. Helen and I have been there recently with a group reunion. And I was coming out of the theater, and I looked at Pike's Peak. And the moment I look there was a big blinding flash, and I thought oh, my God, somebody ran into that. And that's exactly what happened. It was a classmate of mine, Lieutenant Mensees (ph). We don't know what happened or what caused it. We have our own ideas, of course, but he smacked right into it at about the 11 or 12 thousand foot level, I guess. I happened to look up at the peak. It was a lovely sight, Pikes Peak. I saw this orange flame, and I thought oh, my God. So we went up to headquarters and found out who was in that airplane. They said we are finding out now. Later in the evening they announced all the names of the people in it. A terrible accident. They weren't watching. It was night. But we just don't know what happened. We got ides, of course, a lot of suggestions. But one of the suggestions was that they were on auto pilot and the whole crew was gamblers and they went in the back and gambled and playing cards, we thought. But I doubt that. The air crew weren't that stupid. There was something else that went awry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Going back to when you first went into the army. Was it tough to be thrown in there with people from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes, but most of us in those days were mature and well disciplined. You know, black, white, Jewish, gentile, we really didn't care. But today they are -- I think some of these people are educated far beyond their level of intelligence. They will look for any excuse to hate somebody or do something. But, no, I got along rather well. I had no problems. I didn't like what I was doing, unloading boxcars but after that all that was cleared up. And then I had a soft place in my heart for the enlisted men after that. Without them we would be nothing. Absolutely nothing. They took care of our aircraft. They took care of the engines, our guns and bombs and, hell, if it wasn't for them a lot of us wouldn't be here today, and that's the truth. But.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you meet your crew?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: At, again, Peterson Field. We went back in early '44, March. February, March, April of '44, some place in there. Yeah. And we got along reasonably well. There was one man that I wanted to transfer out, but the pilot -- he was a friend of the pilot, so I let it go at that. Got along pretty good. No deaths resulted because of incompetence or anything of that sort. But some crews, they had difficulties, prejudice and whatnot, no question about that. It existed. But, hell, my training was such that I thought I was really well adjusted when I was a teenager. I had a nice mom and dad, brother and sister. Even my dog was nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your plane have a name?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No, it didn't. We couldn't agree on it. And I told the gang, I said okay, name it anything you want as long as it isn't obscene or doesn't upset the colonel. So then we get overseas and the colonel's airplane was named Red Ass. Jake Broger (ph), a wonderful guy. Geez, he was a wonderful guy. He was all right. He was okay. He is still living down in Florida. He is in his late 80s, early 90s, if he is still living. He was in a wheel chair the last I heard. Tall handsome guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go overseas?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, right after that. I missed D day by about a month. We were held in Ireland. I guess we were going to be the second wave or something. I don't know. And the skies were getting full of airplanes at that time, theirs and ours. So that's when we started to launch a thousand bomber raids, and then we had one or two, I think, one or two, 2,000 bomber raids, and I had the good fortune of being on one of those, so historically I thought that was great. I never -- we could get so many airplanes in the air in such a closed area. 2,000 bombers, you consider ten men to a bomber, you have an airborne army of 20,000 men, and each one has got a machine gun, and all those bombs. And then 2,000 fighters went along with us. And they started to put the wing tip tanks on there so they could go the extra two hours. Prior to that we had to go to the target. As soon as we got into enemy territory, the fighters went back. They were low on fuel. And we went in there unattended. But I was sitting up there in the nose turret thinking my God, Belovich, how lucky you are. Look at all these specks. They are all ours. Fantastic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who was the target?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, golly -- Let me get it for you. Three of them got their Ph.Ds, Steven (ph), Vincent, and Stephanie. And Stephanie still lives with us. And Stephanie, for a present for me, did this. She was rummaging around in my footlocker, and she had this T-shirt done.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It is ______ time.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: On the back, she went through my private records and listed all the missions I was on and targets and the dates.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So for the take off your first mission was on the 14th of August of '44?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes, 14th of August of '44. We went through a staging time in Ireland and then in England getting acclimated to color codes and colors of the day and things like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of that first mission?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, only one thing I thought, geez, this is easy. This is simple. This isn't dangerous at all. I was very naive. And that was in France, Dijon, I believe it was. Yeah, Dijon Airfield. But then after that you go to places like this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Those are all Germany?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yes. This was France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Dijon, France?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes. That was on the Loire River.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The 16th of August; and Offenburg, Germany; and Brunswig, Germany, the 24th of August; and Ludwigshafen, 26th of August?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Those are tough targets.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And Ravensburg and Berlin?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: This was a suburb of Berlin, north of Berlin. And Joe Vodka (ph) died on this one here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the Castle raid?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes. There were three Castle raids. And then there were three Cologne raids. I was on those three right in a row. And when you go do something like that the casualties are pretty high in the first one, because on the first one you usually get all the anti-aircraft guns and our fighters take care of their fighters. And the Hamburg raids, I believe there were three of those, if there were ______. I can't remember exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There is the Hamburg raid on the 21st of November, '44?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Marshalls (ph) Yard. That was to destruct their ability to transfer whatever equipment they had over land.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the first mission was on 14 August '44 and the final mission on?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: January 8, '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any good luck charms when you flew?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. Just rosery, being a devote coward, you know. I had a maddening desire to come home in one piece. There were a lot of charming young ladies in Parma where I lived, and I didn't feel I should deprive themselves of my presence. Ego comes to the fore. But then I met Helen, and we got married and educated the kids. And Steven (ph) has his own business now. Lives in Hinckley. And Vincent, he took up the ______ for Air Force. He works as a scientist at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. What he is working on I have no idea. Married and lovely kids. They were here for the holidays.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have when you went to -- Getting back to your first mission, was there a lot of opposition at that time?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No, I don't think so. This is probably why I thought it was easy. Some antiaircraft fire, you see black puffs, and you don't really realize how dangerous those are when they are two- or 300 feet away. But when they get so close they will take six feet of your wing off, then they are pretty close. And there weren't that many fighters, as I recall. Our fighters took care of them. And it wasn't until about -- oh, golly when, I would say October when the fighters were taking their tank -- when they had their extender tanks on and when they could take it right to the target. But then, of course, the enemy fought more tenaciously. They are maniacal. They thought nothing of crashing into you. Actually, the most experienced German pilots were already dead or injured. And the kids now were flying, 18 and 19 years of age. And some of them were taken prisoner. We would hear from ground intelligence that these kids had only had maybe five or ten hours in an FW 190 or an ME 109. They just didn't have the experience. And an airplane like a car will skid, so if you are flying this way and the fighter is coming in and he turns and he doesn't do it quickly enough, he will skid and slam right into you, and they have done that all right just out of stupidity. And this fanaticism that they were told, you know, that they were super human beings and nothing could hurt them. The same as the Iraqis are going through now. Strap a bunch of bombs around you and set yourself off and you are going to get your ten virgins and two cases of wine. They believe that. Simpleminded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were any of them trying to do that on purpose? Were any of them trying to (wrap) wings?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: I would say some was on purpose, right, yeah, but I think a lot of it was just out of sheer stupidity, because, you know, that was the closed society like, again, Iraq. Education was reserved for the middle or upper class. And if you can keep society ignorant, hell, you can tell them to grabble in the dirt and they well. That's how it is. At least that's the way I look at it. They weren't very bright. [Clock chimes] We would get some briefings once in awhile on the German flyers that were captured in France, shot down, or over England. We always had a couple of nuts that would come over after dark and shoot up an air base or something. Or three or four would bail out with machine guns over a small village and go and shoot up the village and die in the attempt. They were that fanatic.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was happening in England?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, certainly, oh, absolutely, yeah. They would shoot up villages.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they were just parachuting in as a terrorist?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Just terrorists, right. And a terrorist is nothing more than a coward, as you know. I don't know why our news media refers to them today as terrorists. They are not terrorists; they are cowards, because they operate by the dark of night and put on baggy clothes and hide the weapons in baggy clothes. That's not being heroic. That is being a coward.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember the first time you realized you were being shot at?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, I said what the hell am I doing here. But when you analyze it in a mature way, you are there for a reason. If you are not there, they are going to be over here, pure and simple. And I have a book in my library to this effect they were planning on bombing New York. Germany was. And they created two four-engine -- no, eight-engine seaplanes, four engines on the side. Weren't gigantic seaplanes. Weren't very fast, about 130, 140, 150 miles an hour. And they would carry enough fuel to go from France across the ocean, sporadically bomb New York, Washington, whatnot, just at random drop the bombs out, turn around and go back over the Indian Ocean and land at a predetermined spot in the ocean and pick up fuel from a German submarine. This was their plan, see. So when we got wind of these things, well, we sent some B-51s out to photograph the area where we thought they were building them, near Dummer Lake, called Dumber Lake, D-u-m-b-e-r, because they weren't very bright. Went over there and shot them up, destroyed them before they could even try anything. But, they were making the effort, see. No question about it. Like Hussein and a few other people. They are actively making an effort. They think they can rule the world. You know, there is some people in this world, Tom, you can give them a gun and a belt full of bullets, and they think they are God, not realizing that hey, that guy out there also has got a gun, see. They can't get it through here. But I was talking to a German prisoner in England. Oh, golly, I was attending this theater in the little village of Bunkie and we had prisoners there who were working on the farms and whatnot. The Italian prisoners only had one Englishman guarding them. The Italians were jovial. They were glad they were out of it. They didn't want to have anything to do with Mussolini and Hitler and whatnot. They were just living a good life. They just wanted to get back to home and their wine. But the Germans were different. They were a real despotic people. They wanted to rule the world. And I was talking to this one Germany sergeant. He was in his late 40s. One of the brightest I met of all of them I talked to. He said when I saw one of your fighter planes come out of the sky, dive down three or four miles to shoot up a private soldier, one of my soldiers on a bicycle, then I knew we lost. And I said how so. That you could take the time and that money and that equipment to kill one man, we lost. I said you are right. And so he was tickled pink he was out of the war. He had a wife and some kids back in Germany. I hope he made it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. As a bombardier you were a nose gunner too?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, right. Because you have to take an extra man, and then that nose gets awful crowded with three or four people up there. You don't want that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever shoot anything?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I shot into the English Channel. I shot at a boat that I knew wasn't ours, but that is about all. You shoot a speck just to keep them away, you know, because when they see the tracers coming at you they will skidaddle. They go out of gun range. They will stand out about 2,000 yards. No, I never got that close. There were some that whizzed by so fast you didn't know. Everybody is yelling in the airplane there goes one, but he cleared you by 100 feet and but he's gone. But three or four seconds he is gone, see. I imagine it must be worse today. But now we have these smart weapons, and they don't call them bombardiers anymore. They call them weapons system officers. And now the situation, Tom, has changed where the WSO, weapons system officer, out ranks the pilot. The pilot is merely the driver, and there is a little, perhaps, a little animosity there. I don't know. But you can't have, if we have to, you can't have a second lieutenant drop the big one. You have to have a senior officer, you know. You can't have --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any targets that you dreaded going after?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, the big ones, the dangerous ones. Oh, like, Castle, Magburg, Hamburg. Oh, my gosh, Cologne. We called it Co-log-ne. And the Germans used to listen on the radio. And I got in a conversation with one. Some of them went to school in the states, you know, under the student exchange plan that we had back in the late '30s. And I happened to get on his frequency or he happened to get on ours. I don't know. To this day I don't know but it happened. There are only so many frequencies, like so many TV stations. And we were talking back and forth. You want to know my name? He was Oberleutnant (ph) or something. I think the equivalent of major. So I had a stroke of genius. I said my name is Goldberg, Sam Goldberg, a Jewish name. And I figured well. Deadly silence on the other end. I thought the SOB signed off. But he didn't. Then he started swearing at me, screaming in English again. And I asked him where did you go to school. And he went to some school in the Carolinas, a military school. The only one I know about there is the Citadel, but there might be more. And he graduated there in 1937 and then went back to Germany to put that knowledge to work. And then he wanted to know where we were at. You know. And I said well, we just bombed the hell out of some of your real estate, just bandied back and forth. And he said what is your altitude. Where are you? We will come kill all of you. What I didn't know, Jake Broger (ph) was listening. And he said knock it off, Belovich. Yes, sir. So then Broger (ph) come on the pipe, and he told them to give the man our altitude and speed, everything where we were at. This is Colonel Jake Broger (ph), commanding officer of 446 Group. We will wait for you. Honest to God. So we had to orbit the area. We flew a race track course. And I thought oh, my God, if they don't kill us my own men will kill me. You know. But it didn't happen that way. We orbited the area. I think we made two big orbits, because you don't want to burn fuel up needlessly. They either were too far away or they didn't have the stomach to duke it out. But Broger (ph) was mad. He said I was hoping for one last battle. We could duke it out with those bastards. But it never happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he was actually waiting for them?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: We were waiting for them, yeah. He was okay. He was a good man. But you love that guy. And he was only about -- He made full colonel when he was 28, and I was 21. So he was only seven years older than I was. So he is 88 or 89, if he is still living now. I hope he is. I hope God takes care of him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memorable missions?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. They are all about the same. In those days, of course, the doctors -- not like now -- you could only fly three missions in a row, and then you were stood down for three or four days to get back to normal. Because flying a mission just isn't on the mission. You have got to get up in 2:30 in the morning and wash and shave, because the beard will grow under your oxygen mask and start leaking, and you can have a problem. And I hated to wear that damn thing. So by the time you got back to the base it was three or four in the afternoon, so you had a good ten or twelve or 14-hour day. You can only do that three days in a row because of the emotional stress and the doctor said no more. Stand them down, so we did. The worse one was Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and the day after. That was during the break out, you know. What was that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During the Bulge, Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, Bulge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the 24th was Breidenbach, 25th was Erlenbach?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Erlenbach, small towns. That's where Germany was amassing tanks and troops, so we carpet bombed the troops which is a horrendous thing to do, but we did it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And Sinzig on the 26th. What's RV stand for?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: RV? RV? What was that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Rail?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Not, not rail. Refinery. I think refinery. I think it was refinery. And here were three more in a row, 26th, 27th, 28th. Hahn, Castle, and Castle, and we were stood down. I was anyway. I think I did that twice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you lost a buddy on one of those Castle raids?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, that was Joe Vodka (ph), on Castle raid. Nice handsome guy. Geez, he had had everything. He had his college out of the way. And he and his girl were going to get married when he got home, and it never came to pass. It is a terrible thing. So he is buried at St. Marys with his mom and dad, same grave. I attended the funeral years and years ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any other buddies on any--

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I don't know what the losses were, I think six or eight percent, something like that sometimes. Or you would go out on a raid. In fact I think one of the Castle raids we lost nine or ten aircraft just out of the group. That is 90 to 100 men. But those are -- Near the end there when I was flying, the Germans, they believed that -- they thought that Freud was God. Whatever Freud even hinted at had to be Christian truth, you know. And they believed firmly that if they would attack one bomber group, destroy it, like they did the Bloody Hundredth, that the rest would be demoralized. Well, not so. You demoralize the remnants of that bomber group, but they will recoup, and they will fight again, see. And they tried that. And then when we had gotten what they were doing, we just had our fighters close at hand just clobber them. We would see airplanes falling like 30 or 40 at a time. Honest to God. But as long as they weren't ours, it was okay. That's how I felt about it. I still do. I will have to find out what that RV was. My memory -- Could be the oil fields, refineries, maybe refinery base, or could be something like that, because they started making synthetic oil, which was very good, by the way. And it didn't burn too -- you couldn't set that on fire too well, but it worked good in lubricating engines and things. We used to -- some of the targets, one was a series of hot houses in France. They had the red cross painted on the hot houses. We thought they were used for hospitals. So we asked the French underground to investigate, and they said hospital, my ass. They are storing fuel in there, ammunition. So we went and shot them up. Oh, my God, did they blow up. Oh, geez, orange flame, black flame. True, they weren't using it for hospitals. But that was again the uneducated, sick mind, you see. If those people had been educated about the Geneva Convention and you don't do these things, they probably wouldn't have done it. And I think that's what we are contending now with in the Mid East.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that's what a hot house was?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, where they grow fruit, vegetables.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, so but it looked like --

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Like you see on Shaff (ph) Road, yeah, that's the hot house. Yeah. And when you shoot up the hot house--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why would they put a red cross on a hot house though?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Well, to make us think it was a hospital.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But still it would be a weird building to have a red cross on it, you think?.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Not necessarily. If the hot house was located in the battle area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they just figured they were using it as a hospital?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Right, exactly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hoping you would figure that --

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah. And when you shoot one up, the glass, it doesn't fall down. It comes up in the air, and it sparkles in the sun, and it is like slow motion. It is really a beautiful sight to see with 50 calibers hitting it, you know. It is a beautiful thing to see.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your Bomb Group again?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 446. And your squadron?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 705 Squadron. Part of the Eighth Air Force?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Part of the Eighth Air Force, yes. I was a first lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: First lieutenant was your rank. Have you been to the Air Force museum? Have you been to the Eighth Air Force museum in Savannah?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No, not Savannah. I have been to those museums in England. Helen and I have gone back about every three years, but we haven't been since the September holocaust. But I hope to go again before I get so old I can't even sit, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like in England back then when you were not flying?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Wonderful. You mean --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Great Britain, right.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: After the war?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, when you were there during the war.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: To keep my sanity, when I was knowing I was going to be stood down for three or four days, I took care of letter writing, my laundry, dry cleaning, and then I would go to the club and have dinner, have a glass of wine with my dinner. English sherry. And then they would say Belovich, where are you going. I am going to walk in the village and get my sanity back. Ah, you are all right, don't sweat it. No, I said, I want to mix with the civilians. So I would walk in the village, Bunkie, a village of about 600 people. Now it has a little over a thousand in it. And they remember us. They call us the Bomber Boys. And I would just walk around there and talk to the people. In fact, I spent a night in an air raid shelter there when the buzz bombs started to come over. I made friends with a family man. He was in his 40s, a wife and three kids. And I tried to find the same house when I was back on one of my trips, but they are all the same. And places have changed, you know, people have gone. And he would be hanging over the fence by the sidewalk. I would be walking out from the base. The village was about a mile from the base, and I enjoyed the walk. Cleared my head. And he would say, Hi, Yank. And I said yes, sir, how are you. And he said fine. He says were you on the big one today. And I said yes, I'm afraid I was. And he said we showed them, didn't we. I said yes, we did. He says I want to thank you for coming over and helping us. We shook hands. A wonderful guy. And I used to smoke a pipe then. And so I lit up my pipe. And he says you ought to try some of my tobacco sometime. And I said oh, next time. I will be walkin' by here quite often. And he says that's great. So next time a couple of days later I brought him a couple of packs of Chesterfield cigarettes. And I gave them to him, because he smoked and his wife smoked, and they loved American cigarettes. So he filled up my pipe pouch with English tobacco. And their tobacco is very aromatic and very mild. The women like that. And, man, I was the toast of the officers club then. Everyone wanted to fall in love with me when I smoked that. Where did you get that, Belovich? I would never tell you. Yes, I would mix with them and attend a movie or just walk around the village, do a little shopping if the store s were open. Have dinner at a little restaurant or have lunch, something to eat. And as I say, a movie or just talk to people. Go in the bar and have a drink. It would be full of GIs, you know. And then go back and get to bed. And the next morning I didn't have to fly. But you would hear the airplanes going over and get up, and you would walk down to headquarters anyway, you know. You just can't get it out of your system, because you get a guilt-pang complex. You should be there. That's what struck me. I should be up there. You know, not letting these green kids, these replacements, do it. But you soon get over that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get any USO shows or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: We had one with Al Jolson. He came over on one of these flatbed tank retriever trucks. And he says what do you think of this English beer. We said yeah, yeah. They ought to put it back in the (wurse), because it was warm beer, you know. I said I don't want to hear that. So I would go to our bar and have a drink. But I didn't drink liquor until I came home. Never touched liquor. I did drink wine and beer, English beer. It was either light or dark and the same temperature, room temperature. They didn't have refrigeration. But they were good people. You go into a pub, which is nothing more than a public house, and the men would be there with their wives and their kids. You don't see that here. Perhaps we should see that here. Maybe there wouldn't be so damn much drunkenness. The kids had a soft drink. They called it an ice over there. They are great people. To this day -- One of the youngsters who would be by my airplane when we landed, John Archer (ph). Wonderful guy. He is in his late 60s, early 70s now. He would come on his bicycle and leave the bike outside the fence and sneak under and be around the airplane. They wanted our escape kids. Have you ever heard what an escape kit is?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. Explain that again.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: It is half round, about this thick and that long, and it would fit in your flying suits and wrapped around your leg. And the escape kit carries some cigarettes; first aid kit; a morphine shot, if you need it; some gum; and maybe about half a day's rations. That was your escape kit. That would tide you over. So I would give my escape kit to everybody. And then the officer would want to know what happened, and I said yeah, it fell out some place. And I thought what the hell. Give it to the damn kids. So I signed off. And he is now a grandfather and a wonderful guy. He shows a lot of souvenirs he picked up around the base, and he remembers us. He doesn't remember me specifically, but he says yeah, there was somebody always passed out goodies for us. And I would caution these kids and say now these cigarettes -- There were four cigarettes, Lucky Strikes, in a little cardboard pack. Make sure your dad or mom gets this. Oh, yeah sure. They are pedaling away on their bike, no hands, and they are lighting up already. Ten or 12 years old. They didn't care. Kids, they were something, you know. Discipline was going down the tube there in the family because all the fathers were back in the service mostly. I had a sad experience. I dated a young lady in Norwich about five or six dates. A lovely little girl. Oh, Gwendolyn Roper (ph), Gwen. And I met her by accident. I was promoted, and she was working in a store for the forces where you could buy anything you needed for any army, allied army, that was in England. And, by golly, there were a lot of allied soldiers in England. So I was buying some first lieutenant bars. This was in September or October, I guess. You get promoted when somebody ahead of you dies. That's about it. Not any particular effort on your part. One of those things. And, so she was -- and she was as white as a sheet. And I was looking out of the corner of my eye, and sitting on this little alcove there was, I found out later, the owner of the store. He had his visor on, and he was going through the point system. They were very strict over there. And he was watching me, and I was talking to her. And he came down and says good afternoon, Lieutenant. And I said good afternoon, sir. And he says I just couldn't help overhearing you were promoted. And I said yes. And he says I wish the Crown would do that with our boys. They go overseas and come back at the same rank. And I said yes, I understand that. There has got to be some reason for it. He says yes, financially we can't do it, but I wish something could be done. And then he looks at the girl and says Gwen. That's where I got her name. Would you be good enough to get the lieutenant a cup of tea and get one for yourself, and do be good enough to get me one too. So we had tea, the three of us. We were chatting back and forth. And then when she went back for something else he says I don't know whether you noticed or not, Lieutenant, but she's not herself. I said yes, she is kind of pale. He said yes. Her dad was killed at El Alamein two years ago, and he's buried there. And the British don't bring their solders back. They are buried there for perpetuity. And her mother was killed two months ago by a buzz bomb attack that hit Norwich. I said oh, my God. And she was an only child. So she is living with an uncle of hers. So I became the perfect gentleman. I invited her out for dinner at the Red Cross club. And the specialty of the night was pork and beans. And weiners. To this day I love pork and beans and weiners. Whenever I have them I think of Gwen. And she said my God, meat. And they call a sausage a banger. You've got to think about that, a banger. So she just wolfed it down. And I asked for seconds. And the Red Cross girl said well, we can do that. I says fine. So then as we were leaving I asked the Red Cross -- the American Red Cross was running it -- could you put another dinner with two hot dogs and beans in a container that I can give this young lady, and she said certainly. And I said I will pay for it, because the Red Cross begs for money. So I gave her a pound note, which was $4 in today's. Hell, I could have bought a ton of those things. But that's another thing. You don't worry about money. What were you going to do it with it? Right. So I sent most of mine home. So I walked her to the bus. And I dated her oh, three or four times after that, and she was coming around. And of course, the buzz bombs, the Germans were firing them sporadically. And you can't aim them. That is why they are so cruel. You can't aim them. They just fly and come down when they are out of fuel. And they would land any place, a school house, an open field, kill a thousand sheep and things like that. And I saw -- I was in a movie with her in Norge -- END OF FIRST FILE; BEGIN SECOND FILE in the old Hay Market Theater, and an air raid siren went off. So the house lights came on. And we moseyed out to the air raid shelters. And there was an air raid shelter right outside. And she dragged me into that, and she was shaking like a leaf. So I put my arm around her and said relax. Everything will be all right. And we sat near the door. So I said to her Gwen, just a moment. I just want to talk to the air raid warden. So I went out, and he put his hand out and said, sorry, Lieutenant. My response. You can't go out. I said I know. But I showed him my wings and said I am a bombardier. He says oh, you are a bomb aimer. So I went out and I heard this purring noise of this beautiful Rolls Royce Merlin. And England come out with a new plane. It was a missile chaser. It was the Typhoon. It swung a five-bladed propeller. When you looked at it you thought you were looking at a wind mill. It had an air scoop big enough to crawl through, because it needed so much air. It was low level piece of equipment. And that Typhoon driver was catching up on this foreign ______ missile. He was really overhauling it fast. And he didn't want to gun it down because it didn't have more than a thousand feet of altitude. So he got his wing under the wing of the missile and tapped it and precessed the gyro and turned it back toward Germany. But of course it never made it, but it went down in the channel. Honest to God. It did a slow roll and went back to patrolling again. You got to see the things to believe it. He really did. He got his wing under it and just tapped it. Because those were gyroscope controlled. You could precess the gyro, and it will level out after a while. And you can precess it again and you can make a complete turn with the thing. Those things will top out at over 500 miles an hour, those Typhoons. They could really move. But the torque on them, because the five-bladed propeller, and that weight -- I bet that propeller probably weighed four- or 500 pounds. It is a gyroscope itself. And I talked to a (rat) pilot who said yeah, he said I never drove one, but I got a friend who does. You have got to cram the rudder way over to the right and (rest) the throttle slowly because even with the rudder crammed over, the airplane will want to waltz off the runway this way, until you get enough forward speed that the controls became effective, because the torque will pull you way right off the runway. And that's what accelerated the development of the jet engine too. We reached the maximum of reciprocating engines. That was it. We had to have some other source of power.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was the Typhoon the size of a fighter basically?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: It was the size of a fighter, but it was a big one. You can tell coming head on -- It was shaped like this. The propeller was up here, and the big air scoop was down here, and the wings were here. It was an ugly-looking thing.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: gooney bird?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: A deadly-looking thing from the front. You didn't want to tangle with a Typhoon. Boy, oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they just used those basically to shoot down --

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: For the missiles, because they could buzz bombs, yeah. The British called it --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Doodle bugs?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Doodle bugs. They called it doodle bugs, yeah, yeah, yeah. And of course the other one, the V-2, they couldn't shoot down, because that was so -- a space flight vehicle, yeah. But then the war ended, and I told her I was leaving and wished her all the luck in the world. She said thank you ever so much. I corresponded with her for a while. I was in school for a while. Because I was reserve and went back into the service during Cuba. I was called back in. Five kids and a screaming wife, and I am back in the service. But, that's the price you pay. I wanted to stay reserve, and I kept my promise.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to go down there and fly around or anything?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. I was a major then. They gave me assistant squadron commander of a B-47 bomber down here in Bomber Basin, southern Ohio. And then after a week later I was made a commander. That's how fast things were operating. And thank God we had the President who had the guts to do something. Otherwise, we would have been gone. We were about 20 minutes from a shoot. I'll never forget that. That's how close we were. I'd say 20 minutes from a shoot. I had men in the aircraft with the engines running. And the fuel going in. We had those quick detachable fuel systems. You fill the wing in from the bottom, put the hose in and turn it 90 degrees. If you have to go, you don't wait for the ground crew to come up and disconnect. You just open the throttle, and it pulls the hose out, and it automatically shuts, and off you go.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess that's when we were waiting to see if the Russians were going to turn around?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yes, right. Then, well, we had a spook. We launched a couple of aircraft. But we called them back by the time they were clearing the north coastal lake area. And then it was all over, and we started breathing easier. But we would have been gone. Thank God. Do it right or don't do it. Get off the pot, you know. So we did it. And a lot of those guys were World War II types too. Geez, there was one guy that was a grandfather. I said what the hell are you doing as a grandfather driving this thing. He said hey, I want to get in my 20 years. I said well, you will get it. That's the way it was. We made bets in the mole hole, the underground place where we used to have briefings, that when this thing was over Khrushchev is going to be dead and Kennedy is going to be dead. They were. Yep. A lot of weird things happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to World War II, do you remember mail call, getting letters, packages from home, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. Sometimes you get the wrong package and whatnot. I used to get my brother's packages. He was stationed there too. And he would get mine. But, yeah, you remember those things. And I especially liked when you didn't fly and you were stood down for two or three days and you were all in the quanset hut and you didn't fly. I think there were 24 officers in our hut, a good-sized hut with two stoves. And you did a lot of BS'ing, and you talk about girls and wives. And sometimes the conversation gets a little raunchy too. You know. And we had a guy there. He was a bombardier. He was a lawyer, about four or five years older than me. Handsome devil. Didn't talk much, but he and I became very good friends. He was a perfect gentleman. He always wore a flying suit and his garrison cap and tie, meticulously dressed. And I think it was one of these, I think the Cologne raid, the third Cologne raid -- probably the first one, because we took such a horrible hit. I would have to check my diary. And I knew we took a big hit. And I come back, and I was the first one in the barracks. And this other bombardier came in about five minutes later, impeccably dressed. And he stopped by my bed. I was reading my mail. He said Belovich, we took a hit today. And he swore. And I said yeah, we sure did, Jack. How many missing? He said, I don't know yet, but there are some stragglers coming in. He says I couldn't wait. I didn't want to stick around. Let the doctors handle it. That's their job. Okay. So he went over to his bed and sat on it. And the orderly put the mail on our bed. And he looked up and said Belovich, she wrote again. Held up a letter. A big beautiful picture of his fiancee on his dresser, in a beautiful stainless steel, highly polished frame. Oh, God, glass and all, with a daring gown. So I am reading a letter from my mom and dad and a pistol goes off. And I instinctively rolled off the bed and had my weapon out, because we were afraid of these cuckoos coming in, shooting up places. And I looked up and looked at him and says what the hell is the matter with you. He said relax, Belovich. He holstered his weapon. I walked over to him and put my weapon away. And he shot his girl's picture. He murdered his girl. There was glass all over. I said what the hell did you do that for. And he hands me the letter. She had found somebody else, a young captain. They were engaged too. And I says the least you could have done is saved the picture frame for me. I could have put my girl's picture in it. So he started laughing. He says damn women. And that's what happened. Yeah, of course the young MP officers come running in and the MPs with their carbines at the ready, because everyone is pretty touchy in those days. It was after D-day. The Germans were trying anything. He stopped by my bed, and I just pointed. It was a captain, short and stocky. And he walked up to the jag, and he says did you fire that weapon. Yep. Give me the weapon. Come and get it. And I thought we were going to have a confrontation here. But the captain wisely backed off. He says well, you are going to have to surrender it to your squadron commander. And he said yeah, that I will. The squadron commander came in a little bit later and says what the hell is going on here, a bunch of kids shooting up the place. And I said sir, it was him. He walked back down there. He walked down there. He busted out laughing. What the hell is the matter with you, Jackie? He gave him the gun back and said sleep it off. Go have a drink on me at the bar. That was it. Murdered her. And left everything there for the cleaning ladies to clean it up later that day. Oh, geez. But the doctor said, Doc Kelly (ph), bless his heart. He was a flight surgeon. He said that was the best thing he could have done, because the tension had built up and he released it with a pistol shot. And that ended his problem. There are more women, you know. And then a day or two later he got a letter from his mother, did you get so and so's letter, because the mother knew about it. And she said I did not want to tell you. I wanted you to find out about it your own way. So his mother handled it beautiful, you know. He was a character. When he walked down the walk from the air base you could tell who he was. He walked straight, tall, meticulously dressed. He was quite a character.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You said you didn't drink, but wasn't it a tradition to get a shot when you --

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, for free, oh, yeah. But I gave mine to my navigator, Bill Snyder (ph), who is still alive and living in Savannah, Georgia. When I last saw him in England he was drunk, and when I saw him at the reunion about eight years ago he was still drunk. Willy is about 83 now. And I was talking to his wife, and she says Tom, he has had so many of his interns taken out, internal body parts, that I don't know how that man lives. And I said well, it's the alcohol preserves him. And she said thank God for that, because, she said, I still like the guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was getting two shots after every mission, right?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah. No, one, and I gave him mine.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what I mean. He had the extra?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: I always told Doc, I said Doc, I will have a glass of wine if I am stood down tomorrow for dinner. And he said good show, Belovich, good show. But the government whiskey had no label on it. It looked like tea, but it was booze. You could tell the guys breathe on you. I think was a good tension reliever, but the men had enough sense if they are going to fly again you shouldn't have alcohol on you for at least 36 hours, because it will impair your ability. No question about it. And, Willy, I never reported him, because this guy was good. He was intuitive. We were never lost. He could lose track or have his equipment blown up or shot up or something, and he knew where we were at. Willy, where are we at? Don't sweat it, Belovich. Don't sweat it. I know where we are at. And he always got us back. Never reported him. But I did sober him up a lot. Set him on the flight deck behind the copilot and stuff an oxygen tube in his mouth and turn it on full bore. We would use up the copilot's oxygen. It took Mack about six missions to find out we were stealing his oxygen. Because they can't function without oxygen. You have to have that. No, Willy was all right. Yeah. He was okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long was your tour of duty at that point?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many missions?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: At that point, I don't know. Probably about 25, 30. I would say 25 or 30, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your last mission?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, do I. Yeah. I left on the 8th of January and didn't get back until the 11th. Knocked down in France. Breaking in a new crew. Broger (ph) asked me to break in a new crew. In the meantime, Broger (ph) was sent home. He was wounded. So I kept my promise, I broke in a new crew, and they almost got me killed. It wasn't their fault. It was just circumstances. Lost super chargers. Lost an engine. We were forced down at an air base in Mereville, France. I remember the call sign, Whiskey Sour. I will never forget it. And the copilot was kind of nervous. I said Mike, punch out the radio. Call Whiskey Sour. They will give us a heading. This thing is going down. Yeah, okay, man. So he punched the radio. He was a flight officer. He punched Whiskey Sour, and they gave us a heading. And that was weird. Went down about 200 feet pulling maximum power on the two good engines. The controller was a sergeant. I went up later and thanked him. He said yeah, I got you on the scope. Keep going straight. He says you are going to see a red school house about two miles right ahead right on the corner. Do a 45-degree to the right. I thought this kid is a clown. I am not in a car. I am in an airplane. But sure enough, there was a brick school house. And Mike heard it too. And the pilot heard it, and they made a 45-degree turn to the right. And he said okay, start letting down. Everything is clear. I didn't see a field. We told him. He said it is there, but it is heavily camouflaged. By the time we came over the fence, suddenly the camouflage, you could see through it. And we landed. It was a little German airfield. And it was littered with aircraft, British, American, German, that were forced-down fighters, bombers, you name it. It was littered, strewn with aircraft. So then they had to send back to base to get the crew to repair it. And I got back in, I think it was the 10th or 11th. I'll have to check my diary. Because they had -- When you don't show up in 24 hours you are listed MIA. So when I got back I sent a cable right away. And told my mother take the service flag out of the window. Junior is coming home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So, when did you come home?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, golly. Again they were holding us there, although I had to clear the base right away. And the colonel did not date my orders. He is a nice guy. So I dissipated myself in London for about ten days and then got on the train and went to the point of embarkation on the west coast. The big one. What the hell was it? The name escapes me now. Liverpool. Liverpool. Got on the boat. It was a nine-day drive back through storms. And we had wounded. It was a hospital ship. We had a lot of wounded on board. An infantry officer. And he lost his left foot at the ankle. He and I became very good friends. Also a chaplain that was sent back, an emotional case. I asked this infantry officer what happened. He stepped on a mine. And he says let's have some fun. And I says how. He says a lot of these guys don't like boats, and they get seasick, and they don't like flying. Do you like pickles? I said yeah. He said let's eat some pickles at lunch. And on these ships they had a little board you pick it up and you slide it this way and it locks in this way and keeps the dishes from falling off. So we served dishes. We did that. Some senior infantry officers were there. And then we started by doing this. He and I. And then we would eat this stuff. And then they would head for the door. And I said we shouldn't do that to these guys. Oh, they need it, you know. Good people, good people. And the chaplain, I felt sorry for him. I thought he was going to jump off the deck. I was sitting on the chair late at night, and he walked over to the deck and kept looking down at the water. I walked over to him and sat down and said having trouble, Chaplain. Oh, hi, Lieutenant. Yeah, a little bit. And he told me the story. He broke under fire. He says I should be helping the people and I couldn't. I said there is nothing to be ashamed of. You were there. That's all that matters. He said they are sending me home. I am going to be discharged. I said don't worry about it. These things happen. I said why don't you go inside. Don't walk too close to the railing. You make me nervous. So he did. He knew what I was trying to say. He was an older man too. He was in his 40s. You know what I liked? I went down in the bowels of that boat. I wanted to see the engine room. Mechanically inclined. And I am looking at a drive shaft and two propeller shafts that are probably two feet in diameter. 90 feet long. I asked the engineer. Disappearing on the ass end of the boat. And the water is coming in through the stuffing boxes, but they had pumps that pumped it out. And I says I have never seen anything like this. He said yeah, this is something, isn't it. The noise was deafening. I says a lot of water coming in. He says oh, that's nothing. He says we have got rough oceans out there. The hull is twisting. He says watch. Hang on. And as the boat went up on the wave and came down in the trough of a sea, the hull twists and the drive shafts suddenly start whirring because there is no resistance. The propeller is out of water. Pick up and go from 90 RPMs to 120 like that. And then when the hull smacks down on the water, the whole thing vibrates again. You can see it readily down there on the keel. And that scared me, but that was normal to them. But water was gushing in, and the pumps were working blowing it back out. But I never saw anything like that in all my life, the big drive shafts. Each screw was turning opposite directions. And those screws are turning constantly, 24 hours a day for nine days. Think about that. And the reason for that was of course, we didn't have to come the straight course for some reason. It was a zigzag course. And it was up to the captain how long you hold the course. He would change it to right ten degrees for 60 seconds and then left 20 degrees for 30 seconds and so forth. So, actually, we probably made a trip and a half across the ocean. But it was a hospital ship. We didn't trust the Krauts at all. They sunk those too. But we had air cover for the first, I think, six or eight hours out, until we were out of range of the patrol boats. But after that we were on our own. But I'm sure the Navy had, six or eight hours out, service vessels and undersea vessels watching us. I'm sure of that. No question about it. They don't tell us everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got home in the spring?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Back home late February of '45. Yeah. They gave me 30 days at home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Wonderful, wonderful, yeah. It was kind of strange. I got on the train at downtown Cleveland about 11:00, and a sergeant helped me. MPs helped me bring my baggage out. I told them don't forget about the foot locker. I will pick that up tomorrow. And I stood in front of the terminal tower about 11:00 at night. All the lights were on, weird, and all the city lit up, but very few people, very little traffic. And I finally haled a cab. And a guy comes up to me. He was a panhandler. He says Lieutenant, give me a dollar. I said I could but I'm not going to. Get yourself a job in the defense plant. They are begging for people. And then he walked away. The first thing. I got home and woke Mom and Dad up. They knew I was on the way already. I had 30 days. And Dad, I had a 1939 Plymouth which I put up on blocks. And by the time I got home Dad had it off the blocks, checked the oil. Had it all greased and tuned it up. Off the blocks, and she was ready. And I had orders to go to Florida, to drive down. In those days you could only drive 35 miles an hour, so they gave me, I think, seven or eight days to drive it. They took good care of us. By that I mean the air corps took good care of the service men in those days. I think they have dropped the ball today. I don't think it is quite as good, although I don't know. I shouldn't question it. But I went down there, and I spent 30 days there, also for psychiatric interview, psychological interviews, medical interviews. They went over you tooth and nail, and then your orders were stamped fit for duty. And mine were, see. So then I knew I would be in the Pacific in six months, because that was the rules and regulations. So I asked for a B-29 and they said yeah, you will get it. And I was breveted a captain over there, but it never caught up to me. It would have had the war gone on. So, that would have been okay, I suppose. But the B-29, again, would carry eight tons of bombs. [clock chimes] And it was a good hundred a miles faster than the other stuff. And I didn't have to wear an oxygen mask. The cabin was pressurized which was great. You weren't encumbered with all that western flying suit and parachute and stuff like that. Everything was close by. You could put it on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You never did have to leave the states after that?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. After that the war ended, and I came home. Then when I left, my old major signed my papers. And he says we will probably be seeing you. I said oh. I didn't think anything of it. And I was walking out the building, and a sergeant ran after me. He says Lieutenant, Lieutenant, sir. And I said what's up. And I said -- looked around and said you don't have to call me sir. Say hey you or Tom. And he said well, the major wants to talk to you. So I walked inside. And I saluted. And he said sit down, Tom. Then he explained to me about the new Air Force. Harry Truman hadn't leaked out in the papers yet, wanted to create a civil Air Force. He said you want to be part of it. I said yeah, why not, see my old buddies. Do a little flying. Why not? There will never be another war. That's how naive I was. We have had a dozen wars since then. So I took the oath and was back in the service in reserve status. We used to fly and used to fly and meet down at old Hopkins Airport and whatnot. Can I get you something to drink, coffee, tea?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I am doing okay. I have one final question, if you have an answer for it. When you think about your experiences during World War II does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, losing a good friend, like Joe. And then a month or so later I lost a cousin of mine, Private First Class Raymond Belovich, my dad's nephew. He was killed in the Battle of the Bulge. And there again, I knew about it, because I sent him a letter, and we corresponded. And I got my same letter back the very next day, saying KIA. And I said oh, my God, Raymond. So I didn't tell my folks, you know, or his folks. That was up to the quartermaster -- not quartermaster but General Hershey, I think, was in charge of personnel. It was up to his office, because we don't want to breach any rules or regulation. Excuse me a minute. I have to hit the plumbing, something upstairs. [Brief recess] BELOVICH: You heard of General Lesley McNair for whom Fort Lesley McNair was named? SWOPE: I believe I have.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: We dropped short, and we killed him in France at the Falaise Gap, F-A-L-A-I-S-E. I don't know why they didn't make a movie out of that. Maybe too much politics involved. But there were panels there on the ground, orange plastic panels that you could see from the air, very vivid. It was clear, and this was in at the breakout in Cannes Sans L'eau (ph), if I recall, back in here some place. And we were going to bomb the troops which is a devastating thing to do. You drop 250 pounders, and you carpet bomb an area. Let's say this table maybe three miles this way and eight miles long. The bombers come over just -- the bombs will land two or three feet apart. Everything in there is dead. Trees. Even rocks are dead. And the panels were laid out to guide us. We dropped, came back. And there was a meeting right away. Briefing was closed. We just killed Leslie McNair and about 90 GIs. I thought oh, my God. And we weren't the only group involved. Most of the Air Force was in on that. We just couldn't believe what the hell we had done. But we all realized that somebody on the ground or somebody in the air made a mistake. The communications. The panels were not in the place where they were supposed to be. So Broger (ph) said yeah, this is true but God damn it, he said, we don't want that. Wait until the people back home find this out. They are going to blame us and call us stupid. And they would of course, and they did eventually. The following day we went out with more bombers to do the same thing, but the panels were moved a little farther up. And damn if we didn't do the same thing again. There was a mistake in locating panels again. To this day I wonder if it was intentional that some people on our side with probably German leanings gave the wrong order and we bombed our troops again. So from that day on high command was somewhat reluctant to carpet bomb unless it was way out, a hundred or 200 miles out. But I often thought historically somebody should do something about that. The Falaise Gap, where we eventually killed about 30 some thousand German troops of the general -- what was the German general? He had guts. He asked Berlin for orders to surrender. And Hitler told him you don't surrender. You stand and die. So he did. But in the end after the second attack he surrendered, and he lived out the rest of his life there in France, because his own people would have killed him. What the hell was his name?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, I have heard -- I don't know if it is part of the same incident -- but part of the problem was the clouds that were kicked up, that they were bombing into the dust clouds?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Well, yes, but we saw the panels.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You could still see the panels?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Dust, oh, sure. We saw the panels.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obviously the panels were wrong?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: This is my objection. They were in the wrong place. Whether it was done intentionally or not, I don't know. But it was a terrible thing. And he was a three star too. General McNair, a nice little guy from what we were told. And plus the other 80 or 90 GIs, that's a biggy. You just don't do that. But we did it, unfortunately. That was tough to live down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There are a lot of guys. Over the time that I have done this, a lot of guys have talked about this, so.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: The Falaise Gap, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No, it wasn't Ludendorff. It is was a common name. But he lived out the rest of his life in France. And the people in France understood, and they protected him. Damn, I can't think of it. But, anyway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not Joe Joe (ph)?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Joe Joe (ph). No. Joe was patronizer. He was a horse's ass. Of course most of them are. Anyone who would obey a stupid order like that. Just like Rommel. Everyone thought Rommel was great. Well, Rommel was a horse's ass. He didn't have to commit suicide. He should have stayed alive and told the truth, but he didn't. He shot himself. We have got to get the truth out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. I drank French wine while in France.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So did your squadron eventually move over to France?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: No. The heavy bombers were kept in England. And the Ninth Air Force, the twin engine bombers were moved to France, as were a lot of fighter units, too, to save those long drives and save on fuel. Heavy bombers were kept in England.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you drink the French wine?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: At Mereville.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were forced down?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah, I met a little -- someday I would like to go to Mereville and see if that bar is still there. And I gave her one of my bars. She wanted to know what that was and I told her. Her dad -- Cute thing. Her dad owned a saloon, but he was a collaborator. I didn't know this until one of the intelligence officers told me about it. And I was -- slept upstairs above the bar. The major, the Italian commander, had his headquarters there. He was the one that told me really. He said watch that son of a bitch, keep your weapon with you. So I went down and had a glass of wine or beer sitting there -- [Interview interrupted by a telephone call.] BELOVICH: Excuse me. Where was I? SWOPE: Let's see, French wine. Or are you talking about the collaborator?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. And there was a gunner from the B-17 sitting by the same table. It was kind of a table about this size. No, it was two tables really. He was sitting up against the wall. And he was nervous as hell. He had a parachute on. He had bailed out. And I said you okay sergeant. He said yes, I think I am okay. And this was January and it was cold. And the sergeant asked the Frenchman, the owner, he said how about putting some more coke on the fire. The Frenchman said no, I don't have any. The kid didn't believe him. You are lying. The bartender kept yelling over and over. The sergeant asked him once more, and he wouldn't do it. So the sergeant got up. The chair he was sitting on, he smashed on the table and put the remains of the chair in the fire. Suddenly, he got the bartender's attention and we got some coke. I said thanks, Sergeant. I wasn't sure how I wanted to handle that. So then we had plenty of heat. Those are little vignettes that make life interesting. Again, I was only 22 at the time and seeing and witnessing all of this. In retrospect I am glad I lived through that, and I am glad I went through it. I wouldn't want to do it again. But at the risk of being egotistical, I played a small part in history, and I am glad of that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life when you got back?

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Yeah. I couldn't stand the corporate mind of the corporate thinking, how little regard they had for a worker, whether the worker was a manager of a facility, as I was a couple of times, or whether you are just a sweeper. I saw, experienced in one company which shall remain nameless, where they spent $87,000 to design a machine so they could fire a black man who was dressed in rubber clothing and rubber gloves washing the acid off of the product by hand. We have got to get rid of that S O B. I said why. Well, we have a machine coming in that is going to do it. So the machine came in, and it wouldn't run. And I thought there is a God, there is a God. So the company I worked for then sent me out there to solve the problem. I couldn't solve the problem. My heart wasn't in it. I asked them to send another engineer out. And about the third or fourth trip I went out there, the machinery was hauled out of the plant, was put in the parking lot to rust away. And then the guy was still there. I patted him on the back when I walked by. Think about that. But then during negotiations the company will look you right in the eye or newspaper's eye or whatever and say labor costs are too high, we can't afford this. Honest to God. I have nothing but contempt for those types. Nothing but contempt. And my sons, Dr. Steve pays his employees well. He is a millionaire. And he follows some of my advise. And Vincent, the same thing at the air base. And Stephanie, she has got her doctorate, and she is a professional at the medical college downtown. And they are following the same philosophy. And we want for nothing. Everything we want we can have or we will get. No problem. We don't have to be hoggish and piggish and deprive a man out of a decent living because we don't like the color of his skin or his religious belief or some damn fool thing. But it is a damn good thing I am okay. I wonder about you, though. Remember that expression?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Or it's in the mail.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Belovich
sp.p: Remember that? Another thing comes to mind during the Cuban Missile Crisis, the tensions were very, very high as you can understand. We are on the border of the brink of self destruction. I don't care what anyone says. We were 20 minutes away from a shoot. That's how close it was. And we spooked a couple of aircraft. I got in my car and drove down to the air base, and I said who launched, who launched. And they said major so and so. And I said oh, God, call them back. We are calling them back. We have certain redundancies where we call them back. This is south of Columbus now. He was going full bore in the B-47. And by the time he cleared the coast of Canada, we got a hold of him and told him it was a spook, false alarm, come back. And he started swearing. And he took that B-47 right under the Mackinaw Bridge. And there is only 90 feet of clearance between the water and the base of the bridge. And he had a black box on board.
